title: Greg Isenberg's 30-step playbook for building an AI-era SaaS company in a niche
summary: Greg lays out a 30-step framework for building a cash-flowing SaaS: pick a subniche, map and manually perform the workflow, turn mechanical steps into agent workflows, and build media and an audience alongside the product. He ends with moving from per-seat to per-task and outcome pricing, building switching costs through data and memory, and becoming the default execution layer for the niche.

principles.text: Start with a subniche inside a big market, not the big market itself, and aim for a cash-flowing business.
principles.quote: don't make the don't make a mistake of trying to build something for a huge market because that's where the venture boys are playing.

principles.text: Map the niche's workflow end to end and mark where money changes hands; that is where your software wedge lives.
principles.quote: where money changes hands, i.e. you know, in this example, negotiate scope or price, collect deposit, order materials for suppliers. That's where you're going to be able to create some like wedge in software

principles.text: Quantify the value of repetitive steps in time and money to price and sell the automation.
principles.quote: if you can say, "Hey, I'm going to save you 50 hours of time this year, 100 hours of time this year, 150 hours of time this year. What's that worth it to you?"

principles.text: Build media, not just a product: pick one channel, study what earns saves/replies/DMs, then run paid ads on proven organic winners.
principles.quote: you're not just going to want to create a product, my friends. No, no, no, no, no. You're going to want to create media.

principles.text: Start by doing the workflow manually (service first), then separate judgment from mechanical tasks and automate the mechanical ones with agents.
principles.quote: a lot of these future of SAS businesses are actually going to start off as service businesses with human beings at the core of it.

principles.text: Move pricing from per seat to per task to outcome pricing, then raise prices as value compounds.
principles.quote: eventually you're going to want to make your way to a per task basis. And that's going to shift you step 22 to outcome pricing.
